legal.title: lib/legal.ts COMPANY constant is the brand, hardcoded, and never reads config.company
legal.evidence: Line 22: `const COMPANY = "RoutePlanner";` — the file's only import is line 1 `import type { Locale } from "@/lib/i18n";`. It never imports `@/lib/config`, and `grep -rn "company.legalName|company\.idNumber|company\.address" src` returns hits only in `src/lib/contract.ts` (lines 89-91, 129-131, 354-355). The strings "Route Georgia", "405773322" and "Vazha-Pshavela" do not appear anywhere in src/lib/legal.ts or src/app/[locale]/legal/[slug]/page.tsx.
legal.why: COMPANY is the token substituted into the two documents that identify a legal party: the terms intro (line 36) and the privacy intro (line 122). In both positions the reader must be told which registered entity is speaking. "RoutePlanner" is the brand travellers see; it is not a legal person, cannot be looked up in the Georgian register, and cannot be served or sued. Now that COMPANY_LEGAL_NAME/ID/ADDRESS are populated, the legal pages are the one public surface still frozen on the brand.
legal.fix: Import config into src/lib/legal.ts and stop hardcoding a single token. Keep a brand constant for narrative sentences, and add entity fields for the identification passages: `const COMPANY = "RoutePlanner";` plus `const ENTITY = config.company.legalName;`, `const ENTITY_ID = config.company.idNumber;`, `const ENTITY_ADDRESS = config.company.address;`. Since legal.ts is imported by a server component only, the config import is safe.

legal.title: Privacy notice never names the data controller (no legal name, ID number or registered address)
legal.evidence: Intro, lines 122-124: "This describes exactly what ${COMPANY} stores, why, who can see it and how long we keep it." — i.e. "This describes exactly what RoutePlanner stores...". The document's six sections (lines 125-188) never identify a controller. The nearest thing to controller contact detail is line 172: "Write to ${CONTACT}" (support@routeplanner.ge), and line 174 asserts "Georgia's Law on Personal Data Protection applies to us. If you are in the EU or UK, GDPR rights may also apply to you." — a statement that a controller-identification duty applies, in a document that then does not discharge it.
legal.why: A privacy notice must identify the data controller as a legal person: the entity that decides purposes and means, receives access/erasure requests, and is answerable to the supervisory authority. The notice itself invokes the Georgian personal-data law and GDPR (line 174), both of which require the controller's identity and contact details be given to the data subject. A brand name gives a data subject no one to address a request to and no one for a regulator to name. The document also collects a large volume of identifiable data (lines 129-135: name, email, phone, exact pickup and drop-off addresses, flight number, free-text notes) plus driver identity documents (lines 141-143), which makes the omission substantive rather than formal.
legal.fix: Add a controller-identification block as the first section of the privacy document (or extend the intro), naming all three values from config: e.g. a section `heading: "Who is responsible for your data"` with body `` `The data controller is ${ENTITY} (identification number ${ENTITY_ID}), registered at ${ENTITY_ADDRESS}. ${COMPANY} is the trading name of that company.` `` and repeat the entity in the "Your rights" section at line 172 so the erasure/access request has a named addressee alongside ${CONTACT}.

legal.title: Terms of service never name the contracting party — no legal name, ID number or registered address
legal.evidence: Intro, lines 36-38: "${COMPANY} is a marketplace. We introduce travellers to independent private drivers in Georgia, take the booking, and support both sides. We are not the carrier..." — renders as "RoutePlanner is a marketplace." The eight sections that follow (lines 39-113) speak entirely as an unidentified "we": "We take the booking, hold the agreed price" (line 52), "We charge drivers a commission" (line 75), "We may suspend an account" (line 96), and the Liability section (lines 100-108) "Our responsibility is for the service we provide". The closing "Contact" section (lines 110-112) is a single line: "Write to ${CONTACT} and a person will answer." — an email address, no registered address.
legal.why: These terms are the contract between the traveller and the platform: they allocate liability (lines 100-108), reserve a right to suspend accounts (line 96), and bind the platform to hold a price and refund. A contract's counterparty must be an identifiable legal person. As written, the traveller's counterparty is a brand, so there is no named party to hold to the liability clause and no registered address for service of notice or claim. This is the same identification the driver and school contracts already carry via placeholders() in lib/contract.ts — the public terms are the outlier.
legal.fix: Name the entity in the terms intro and give it a registered address in the Contact section. Intro: `` `${COMPANY} is a marketplace operated by ${ENTITY} (identification number ${ENTITY_ID}), registered at ${ENTITY_ADDRESS}. In these terms "we" means ${ENTITY}.` `` before the existing "We introduce travellers..." sentence. Contact section (line 111): add the registered postal address alongside ${CONTACT}.

legal.title: Booking confirmation page — the only post-payment surface — never names the entity that took the money
legal.evidence:
The payment card is the whole of the financial disclosure:

{t("booking.paymentT")}

{formatMoney(gross, booking.currency, locale)}

{booking.payment_mode === "CASH" ? t("booking.cashDue") : t("booking.paidOnline")}

Those two strings resolve to "Cash to the driver at the end of the trip." and "Paid online by card." (src/lib/i18n/en.ts:349-350). The page imports config (line 8) but uses it only for config.policy.version in the cancellation-policy query (line 77) — config.company is never read. Nothing on the page, in any of its three cards, carries a legal name, identification number or address. The cancellation card (lines 192-204) promises a fee or a free cancellation without naming who charges or refunds it.
legal.why: This is the page a traveller lands on after paying and the page the manage-link in their email points to (booking.ts:239, manageUrl). It is the customer's only durable record of the transaction. The party that took the money and owes the refund is LLC Route Georgia, ID 405773322 — not the brand. A payment record that identifies no legal person is not a record a customer can act on with a bank, a card issuer or a court, and Georgian consumer/e-commerce practice expects the supplier to be identifiable on the transaction record.
legal.fix: Add an issuer block to the payment Card: config.company.legalName, "ID <config.company.idNumber>", config.company.address, plus the booking code and date — rendered for both CASH and CARD. This is the minimum that turns the page into a usable receipt.

legal.title: Customer confirmation email is the de-facto receipt and carries no sender entity in any of the three locales
legal.evidence:
confirmedBody (en) is the complete customer-facing email:

  confirmedBody: (b: BookingSummary, price: string, l: Locale) => [
    `Your driver is confirmed.`, ``,
    `Booking reference: ${b.code}`,
    ...
    `Price: ${price} for the whole vehicle`,
    b.paymentMode === "CASH"
      ? `Payment: cash to the driver at the end of the trip.`
      : `Payment: paid online. Nothing to pay the driver.`,
    ...
    `Free cancellation. We ask for at least 24 hours' notice where possible.`,
  ],

The ka body (lines 486-502) and ru body (lines 534-550) are identical in structure and also end with the cancellation line — no signature, no company block. Contrast the driver bodies, which at least sign off with a URL (line 466). Neither transport appends anything: resendTransport sends `text: message.body` verbatim (line 127) and smtpTransport likewise (line 176); the only identity on the message is the From header, config.mail.from, which defaults to "RoutePlanner <noreply@routeplanner.ge>" (src/lib/config.ts:91) — brand, not entity.
legal.why: This email states a price and a payment status and is what a traveller keeps and forwards to an employer or an insurer. It is the closest thing to a receipt the system produces, and it identifies no legal person as the recipient of the payment. Note the file already imports config (used at line 466 for appUrl), so the entity is one property access away.
legal.fix: Append a fixed footer to confirmedBody in all three locales: `${config.company.legalName} · ID ${config.company.idNumber} · ${config.company.address}` (with the Georgian rendering for ka). Do the same for cancelBody, which announces a refund.

legal.title: No receipt or invoice document exists anywhere in the codebase
legal.evidence:
A case-insensitive search for invoice/receipt across all of src/ returns no document generator — only src/app/admin/actions.ts:724 (an admin free-text field: "bank reference, receipt number, or 'cash in office'"), src/lib/notifications.ts:78 (an SMS delivery receipt), a comment in src/lib/config.ts:97, and marketing copy at src/lib/i18n/ka.ts:604-605 promising businesses "ერთი შეთანხმება, მარტივი ინვოისინგი" (one agreement, simple invoicing).

The money is nonetheless fully recorded: ledger.ts:19-23 defines CARD_CLEARING ("money the payment provider holds for us"), PLATFORM_REVENUE ("commission, earned") and DRIVER_PAYABLE, and booking.ts posts against them inside the booking transaction. The platform books its own revenue but issues the payer nothing.
legal.why: A card payment is taken by the registered entity, and the commission recorded as PLATFORM_REVENUE is that entity's taxable income. A Georgian business taking payment must be able to produce a document naming itself and its identification code (405773322) against that income. Right now a paying customer cannot obtain one by any route in the product — not on the page, not by email, not on request. The business page also promises corporate clients invoicing that does not exist.
legal.fix: Add a receipt surface — a printable /booking/[code]/receipt route or a PDF attached to the confirmation email — headed with config.company.legalName, the identification number, the address, the booking code, the service date, the gross amount and the payment method. The ledger already holds every figure it needs.

legal.title: Terms of service names the brand as the contracting party; the entity appears nowhere in it
legal.evidence:
const COMPANY = "RoutePlanner";

It is then substituted into the operative sentences of the agreement, e.g. line 35:

  intro:
    `${COMPANY} is a marketplace. We introduce travellers to independent private drivers ` +
    `in Georgia, take the booking, and support both sides. We are not the carrier: ...`

and throughout the "What we do and do not do", "Payment" and "Liability" sections (lines 45-105), which allocate responsibility, disclaim carrier status and describe commission — all attributed to "RoutePlanner". config is never imported into legal.ts. The document has no party-identification block: no legal name, no identification code, no registered address.

This is the document the customer is made to accept in order to pay: src/app/[locale]/checkout/form.tsx:155-160 renders a required checkbox labelled t("checkout.terms") = "I accept the terms of service and privacy notice..." (src/lib/i18n/en.ts:282), and src/lib/booking.ts:102 refuses the booking without it.
legal.why: This is the strongest instance of brand-standing-in-for-entity in the repo. A contract that limits liability, disclaims carrier status and allocates responsibility must name the legal person bound by it; "RoutePlanner" is a trading name and cannot be sued or hold obligations. Every disclaimer in the Liability section is being made by an entity the reader is never told exists. The file's own header comment says the copy was written "rather than being a template with the company name substituted in" — the company name is exactly what is missing.
legal.fix: Import config in legal.ts and open the terms with an identification of the party: `${config.company.legalName} (identification code ${config.company.idNumber}), ${config.company.address}, trading as RoutePlanner`. Keep "RoutePlanner" for the ordinary narrative sentences after that — brand in prose, entity as the named party.

legal.title: Privacy notice identifies no data controller
legal.evidence:
intro:
  `This describes exactly what ${COMPANY} stores, why, who can see it and how long we ` +
  `keep it. ...`

The notice goes on to invoke the applicable law directly at lines 172-174: "Georgia's Law on Personal Data Protection applies to us. If you are in the EU or UK, GDPR rights may also apply to you." The rights section (line 170) directs subject-access, rectification and erasure requests to `${CONTACT}` — support@routeplanner.ge (line 23) — with no controller name and no postal address anywhere in the document.
legal.why: Both regimes named in the notice require the controller to be identified by legal identity and contact details; a data subject exercising a right must know which legal person they are addressing. Naming only the brand means the notice cites its own governing law and then fails the identification that law requires. The registered address is now available as config.company.address.
legal.fix: Add a "Who is responsible for your data" section naming config.company.legalName, its identification number and config.company.address as the controller, alongside the existing support address.

legal.title: Site footer credits only the brand — no operator identification on any page
legal.evidence:
© {new Date().getFullYear()} {t("brand.name")}

rendering "© 2026 RoutePlanner" (brand.name = "RoutePlanner", src/lib/i18n/en.ts:13). The footer's contact block above it (lines 136-141) prints config.contact.phone and config.contact.email only, and the descriptive line at 142 is t("footer.preLaunch") = "Built in Tbilisi. RoutePlanner connects travellers directly with vetted local drivers." The layout imports config (used for contact) but never reads config.company.

As it stands there is no page in the entire product on which a visitor can learn who they are transacting with. This is the cheapest single fix in the list and it covers the checkout page, where the customer is deciding whether to hand over money.

legal.title: No transactional email carries any company identification — config.company is never read outside contract.ts
legal.evidence: The template table `const M = {` at line 429 spans every customer- and driver-facing message (confirmedBody, driverBody, cancelBody, reviewBody in en/ka/ru, lines 430-580) and no branch ends in a signature or footer. The English confirmation's last line is `` `Free cancellation. We ask for at least 24 hours' notice where possible.` `` (line 452); the review invitation's last line is `` `This link works once and expires in 30 days.` `` (line 479). notifications.ts imports `config` at line 6 and uses it only for `config.mail.*`, `config.sms.*` and `config.appUrl` — grep for `config.company` across src/ returns hits in exactly two files, src/lib/contract.ts (lines 89-91, 129-131, 354-355) and the comment in src/lib/config.ts:102. Nothing in the mail path.
legal.why: Outside the four contract PDFs, a recipient of anything RoutePlanner sends — booking confirmation, cancellation, driver assignment, review invitation, password reset, applicant welcome — sees no legal name, no ID number, no registered address. The registered entity is required to be identifiable in the commercial communications it sends, and the config.ts comment at line 97 acknowledges the same details are "required on a Georgian invoice". Right now the entity is discoverable only by a driver who opens the contract page; a traveller who books, pays and is refunded never learns who they transacted with, and has no name to put on a complaint or a claim.
legal.fix: Add one footer helper in notifications.ts, e.g. `const signature = (l: Locale) => [``, `—`, config.company.legalName, `ID ${config.company.idNumber}`, config.company.address, config.contact.email].join("\n")`, and append it to every EMAIL body in M and at the other queue sites (src/lib/auth/reset.ts:52, src/lib/driver-application.ts:424/441/458, src/app/admin/actions.ts:145). Leave SMS bodies alone — 160 characters cannot carry it.

legal.title: The refund notice — the traveller's only record of money returned — names no entity
legal.evidence:
subject: `Refund issued for booking ${booking.code}`,
      body: [
        `We have issued a refund of ${(Number(input.amountMinor) / 100).toFixed(2)} ${booking.currency}` +
        ` for booking ${booking.code}.`,
        ``,
        `Reason: ${input.reason}`,

          ? `It returns to the card you paid with. Banks usually take 5–10 working days.`
          : `Our team will contact you to arrange the transfer.`,

legal.why: A refund confirmation is a financial record a traveller keeps and may present to their bank in a chargeback dispute, and for a cash booking it is a written promise that "our team will contact you to arrange the transfer" — an undertaking to pay, made by nobody in particular. "We" here is an unnamed party. This is the same class of document config.ts:97 calls out as needing the company details ("required on a Georgian invoice"), and it is the money-bearing message in the whole set.
legal.fix: Append the company footer to this body, and name the payer explicitly in the cash branch: `${config.company.legalName} will contact you to arrange the transfer.`

legal.title: Footer publishes no legal name, registration number or registered address anywhere on the site
legal.evidence:
The whole footer (lines 131-199) contains four columns and a bottom bar. The only identity-bearing content is `` (line 134), `{t("brand.tagline")}` (line 135), `config.contact.phone` (line 138), `config.contact.email` (line 140), `{t("footer.preLaunch")}` (line 142) — which resolves to "Built in Tbilisi. RoutePlanner connects travellers directly with vetted local drivers." (src/lib/i18n/en.ts:548) — and the bottom bar `

© {new Date().getFullYear()} {t("brand.name")}

` (line 185). `config` is imported at line 7 but only `config.contact.*` is read; `config.company` never appears in this file. A repo-wide grep for `company.legalName|company.idNumber|company.address|COMPANY_LEGAL_NAME|COMPANY_ID_NUMBER|COMPANY_ADDRESS|Route Georgia|405773322|Vazha-Pshavela` across src/ returns hits in exactly two files: src/lib/config.ts (the definitions) and src/lib/contract.ts (lines 89-91, 129-131, 354-355). Nothing outside the driver/school contract renderer ever names the entity.
legal.why: Georgian company law (and the EU e-Commerce Directive regime the site's EU-facing traffic invites, plus Georgia's own Law of Entrepreneurs) requires a trading company to publish its legal name, identification number and registered address on its website in a permanently accessible, easily identifiable form — the footer is the conventional place. The site currently identifies itself to the public solely as "RoutePlanner", a brand with no legal existence. A traveller who wants to know who they are contracting with, serve notice, or file a claim cannot learn it from the site at all: the entity appears only inside a signed driver or school agreement, which travellers never see. The values are already loaded and correct in config.company — they are simply never rendered on any public page.
legal.fix:
Add an identity block to the footer's first column, after the contact details and before/around footer.preLaunch, reading the values already available on the imported config: e.g. `

{config.company.legalName}

ID {config.company.idNumber}

{config.company.address}

` in the small pine-300 text style. Guard each on a non-empty value so a future blank env override degrades rather than printing a stray label.

legal.title: Footer copyright line asserts the brand, not the entity that owns the copyright
legal.evidence:
`

© {new Date().getFullYear()} {t("brand.name")}

` — and `"brand.name": "RoutePlanner"` in src/lib/i18n/en.ts:13, src/lib/i18n/ka.ts:8 and src/lib/i18n/ru.ts:8. The rendered line is "© 2026 RoutePlanner".
legal.why: A copyright notice names the rights holder, which is a legal person. "RoutePlanner" is a trading name that cannot hold rights; LLC Route Georgia can. This is the one line on every page of the site whose entire job is to name the owning entity, and it names the brand instead. It is also the line most readers scan for the company's identity, so getting it right partly mitigates the missing-imprint problem above.
legal.fix: Render `© {year} {config.company.legalName}` (falling back to `t("brand.name")` only if legalName is empty). Keep `t("brand.name")` for the logo, nav aria-label and marketing copy — those are correctly the brand.

legal.title: Terms of service name "RoutePlanner" as the contracting party
legal.evidence: `const COMPANY = "RoutePlanner";` (line 22), used at line 36 in the terms intro: "`${COMPANY} is a marketplace. We introduce travellers to independent private drivers in Georgia, take the booking, and support both sides. We are not the carrier...`". The file's own header comment (lines 4-12) says the documents describe "what this software actually does ... rather than being a template with the company name substituted in". This module is imported by src/app/[locale]/legal/[slug]/page.tsx:5 and rendered publicly at /{locale}/legal/terms.
legal.why: The terms of service are the traveller-facing contract — the counterparty of every booking. They currently identify that counterparty as a brand with no legal existence, and give no registration number or registered address for it, so the document names no one who can be sued or served. This is the same defect the driver and school agreements were just fixed for; the customer-side contract was left on a hardcoded brand string and does not read config.company at all (config is not imported in this file).
legal.fix: Import `config` from "@/lib/config" and replace the `COMPANY` constant with `config.company.legalName`, or introduce the entity explicitly on first use — e.g. `${config.company.legalName} ("RoutePlanner"), ID ${config.company.idNumber}, ${config.company.address}, is a marketplace...` — then continue using the brand for the rest of the copy. Also replace the hardcoded `CONTACT` (line 23) with `config.contact.email` while there.

legal.title: Privacy notice does not identify the data controller
legal.evidence: Privacy intro (lines 121-124): "`This describes exactly what ${COMPANY} stores, why, who can see it and how long we keep it.`" — resolving to "RoutePlanner". The "Your rights" section (lines 168-175) says "Write to ${CONTACT}" (support@routeplanner.ge) and "Georgia's Law on Personal Data Protection applies to us. If you are in the EU or UK, GDPR rights may also apply to you." No legal name, identification number or registered address appears anywhere in the privacy document.
legal.why: Both regimes the notice itself invokes require the controller to be identified by name and contact details: GDPR Art. 13(1)(a), and the Georgian Law on Personal Data Protection's equivalent transparency duty. "RoutePlanner" is not a legal person and cannot be a controller, so a data subject exercising access or erasure — or the supervisory authority acting on a complaint — has no identified entity to address. A support mailbox is not a substitute for the controller's identity and registered address.
legal.fix: Add the controller identity to the privacy notice: name LLC Route Georgia, its identification number and its registered address (from config.company) in the intro or in a dedicated "Who we are" section, and repeat the registered address alongside the support email in "Your rights".

legal.title: Terms "Contact" section gives only a support mailbox, no entity or registered address
legal.evidence:
```
heading: "Contact",
body: [`Write to ${CONTACT} and a person will answer.`],
```
where `const CONTACT = "support@routeplanner.ge";` (line 23). This is the closing section of the terms of service.
legal.why: The contact section of a trading company's terms is where the entity's postal address and registration details are normally required to be reachable — an email address alone does not let a customer serve formal notice, and consumer-protection disclosure expects a geographic address for the trader. The registered address is available in config.company.address and is not printed on any public page.
legal.fix: Extend the Contact section body to include the entity line: legal name, ID number and registered address from config.company, alongside the support email.

legal.title: Contact page — the natural imprint page — carries no company identity, and hardcodes the support email it claims to centralise
legal.evidence: Lines 24-30: a comment reading "Contact details are held in one place so they cannot drift between the footer, the emails and this page." followed by `const SUPPORT_EMAIL = "support@routeplanner.ge";` and `const SUPPORT_HOURS = "Every day, 08:00 – 22:00 Georgia time";`. `config` is imported (line 5) but used only for `config.appUrl` in generateMetadata (lines 18-19). The page renders four Cards (lines 48-83) and a legal-links list (lines 86-102); no legal name, ID number or address appears. SUPPORT_HOURS is declared and never used — the hours come from `t("contact.hours")` at line 64.
legal.why: "Contact" is where a reader who wants the company's real identity and postal address will look after the footer, and in many jurisdictions the imprint duty is satisfied on precisely this page. It gives an email and support hours only. Separately, the hardcoded SUPPORT_EMAIL contradicts the comment above it and drifts from `config.contact.email` (the footer at layout.tsx:140 uses config), so the two can diverge the moment SUPPORT_EMAIL env is set.
legal.fix: Add a "Company" card or a closing block listing `config.company.legalName`, `ID {config.company.idNumber}` and `config.company.address`. While editing, replace the local SUPPORT_EMAIL with `config.contact.email` and delete the unused SUPPORT_HOURS constant.

legal.title: HANDOVER.md documents a different company identification number than the one now configured
legal.evidence: | `COMPANY_ID_NUMBER` | Printed in every contract | `437377704` |  — while src/lib/config.ts:106 reads `COMPANY_ID_NUMBER: z.string().default("405773322"),`
legal.why: HANDOVER.md section 10 is the environment-variable table the person standing up the on-premise host works from, and section 13 points at it as the authority. Anyone following it will set COMPANY_ID_NUMBER=437377704 in the new environment; the env var overrides the default, so every driver and school agreement signed on that host would name LLC Route Georgia with an identification number that is not its own. An identification code is how the counterparty in a Georgian agreement is identified at all — a wrong one is not a typo, it is the wrong legal person.
legal.fix: Change the note in the HANDOVER.md table to `405773322`, or drop the value from the table and say the number is defaulted in src/lib/config.ts so there is one source. If 437377704 is genuinely the registered code, then config.ts:106 is the wrong one and this must be resolved against the registry extract before any further signing.

legal.title: .env.example sets all three COMPANY_* variables to empty string, which overrides the new defaults
legal.evidence: Lines 42-47: "# ---- Contracting entity ----" / "# Printed into the driver agreement. The agreement cannot be published for" / "# signature until all three are set — see src/lib/contract.ts." / `COMPANY_LEGAL_NAME=""` / `COMPANY_ID_NUMBER=""` / `COMPANY_ADDRESS=""`
legal.why: The defaults in config.ts are Zod `.default()`, which only applies when the variable is undefined. `COMPANY_LEGAL_NAME=""` makes it defined-and-empty, so the default never fires. The file's own instruction is to copy it to .env (config.ts:126: "Copy .env.example to .env and fill it in."), so following it silently reverts the registered entity to blank: missingCompanyDetails() (src/lib/contract.ts:88-92) starts returning all three again and no driver can be published. The comment above the block is also now false — the details are set, not "until the company is registered".
legal.fix: Comment the three lines out (`# COMPANY_LEGAL_NAME="LLC Route Georgia"` etc., as the S3 block at lines 35-40 already does) and rewrite the header comment to say the entity is defaulted in src/lib/config.ts and these override only for a rename or a move.

legal.title: Georgian-language agreements render the entity name in Latin script; there is no Georgian legal-name setting
legal.evidence: placeholders() takes `locale: ContractLocale` yet maps the name locale-independently: `COMPANY_LEGAL_NAME: config.company.legalName,` (line 129) with a single value `"LLC Route Georgia"` (src/lib/config.ts:105). tests/contract-render.test.ts:17 shows the Georgian registered form exists: `process.env.COMPANY_LEGAL_NAME ||= 'შპს "რაუტ ჯორჯია"';`
legal.why: The ka driver and school agreements are the ones actually signed in Georgia, and they will now name the counterparty as "LLC Route Georgia" inside otherwise Georgian text, with an English street address ("Vazha-Pshavela 76, Tbilisi, Georgia") beside it. The registered form in the Georgian registry is შპს "რაუტ ჯორჯია"; an agreement that identifies its own party in a transliteration rather than the registered form is exactly the kind of defect a dispute turns on. Every other locale-varying value in placeholders() (SETTLEMENT_PERIOD, via settlementPeriodLabel(…, locale)) is already resolved per locale, so the mechanism exists and only the company details bypass it.
legal.fix: Add COMPANY_LEGAL_NAME_KA and COMPANY_ADDRESS_KA to the schema in src/lib/config.ts (defaulting to the registered Georgian forms), expose them under config.company, and select on `locale` in placeholders() the way settlementPeriodLabel already does. Have missingCompanyDetails() gate on the ka pair too, since ka is the locale that signs.

legal.title: src/lib/legal.ts identifies the site to travellers by brand only, with no registered entity in the terms or privacy policy
legal.evidence: `const COMPANY = "RoutePlanner";` and `const CONTACT = "support@routeplanner.ge";` — used at line 36 ("`${COMPANY} is a marketplace...`", the opening of the Terms of service) and line 122 ("`This describes exactly what ${COMPANY} stores, why, who can see it and how long we `", the privacy policy). config.company is never imported here; a grep for config.company across src returns only src/lib/contract.ts.
legal.why: The terms of service are the contract with the traveller and the privacy policy names the data controller — both need the party that can be sued and the party registered as controller, i.e. LLC Route Georgia, ID 405773322, Vazha-Pshavela 76. "RoutePlanner" is the brand and appears in no registry. Now that config.company holds real values this is a one-line fix that was impossible before; the file's own header comment (lines 3-12) says a Georgian lawyer must review it, and the missing entity is the first thing such a review returns.
legal.fix: Import config into src/lib/legal.ts and give the documents an entity line — keep ${COMPANY} for the ordinary brand voice but open the terms and the privacy policy with `${config.company.legalName} (identification code ${config.company.idNumber}), ${config.company.address}, trading as RoutePlanner`.

trust.title: Cancellation policy promises refunds without identifying who owes them
trust.evidence: Intro, lines 196-199: "Cancellation is currently free of charge. This page records the policy in force so that a booking made today is judged by the rules that applied today..." — unlike terms and privacy it does not even interpolate ${COMPANY}. The refund obligations are all unattributed "we": "We find you an equivalent or better replacement at the price you already agreed. If the replacement charges more, we absorb the difference." (lines 214-215), "If we cannot find one, you are refunded in full and pay nothing." (line 216), "we will move your trip or refund it in full" (line 232).
trust.why: This page states standalone monetary obligations — absorbing a price difference, refunding in full — and is explicitly framed at lines 197-199 as the terms in force at booking time, so it is contractual. A money obligation with no named obligor is unenforceable against anyone in particular. Lower severity than terms and privacy only because a reader can chain to the terms; the fix is to close that chain.
trust.fix: Interpolate the entity once in the cancellation intro so the obligor is named on the page itself: e.g. `` `Cancellation is currently free of charge. This policy forms part of your agreement with ${ENTITY} (identification number ${ENTITY_ID}) and records the policy in force...` ``

trust.title: The legal page template renders no company identification, so no page-level footer supplies the missing entity
trust.evidence: The component imports config at line 40 (`import { config } from "@/lib/config";`) but uses it only for URLs — line 60 `canonical: \`${config.appUrl}/${locale}/legal/${slug}\`` and line 61 languages. The rendered tree (lines 73-121) emits breadcrumb, title, `Last updated {doc.updated}`, `{doc.intro}`, the unreviewed-by-counsel Alert (lines 88-93), `doc.sections`, and a nav of sibling links plus Contact (line 118). Nothing reads config.company. Grep confirms config.company is consumed only in src/lib/contract.ts.
trust.why: This matters because it forecloses the usual escape hatch: on many sites the entity, ID and registered address appear in an imprint or page footer even when the body copy omits them, which can cure a missing controller identity. Here the legal route renders only the document object from lib/legal.ts, so whatever that module omits is absent from the page entirely. It also shows the fix belongs in lib/legal.ts rather than the template — with one caveat below.
trust.fix: Either add an imprint block to this template rendering `config.company.legalName`, `idNumber` and `address` beneath the sections (which also covers the DB-override path), or fix lib/legal.ts as described above. Prefer the template block in addition, because getOverride (lines 14-39) lets a published content_pages row replace the code default wholesale — an editor pasting lawyer-reviewed text can silently drop the entity identification again, and a template-level imprint survives that.

trust.title: Contact page publishes no registered address although one is now configured
trust.why: A page titled "Contact and support", on a site that takes money, gives an email address and opening hours but no physical address for the entity behind it — even though config.company.address is now populated with Vazha-Pshavela 76, Tbilisi. A customer with a formal complaint, a chargeback dispute or a legal notice to serve has no address to send it to. The comment's own claim about a single source of truth is undercut: this page hardcodes contacts rather than reading config.
trust.fix: Add a card identifying the operator — config.company.legalName, identification code, config.company.address — and switch SUPPORT_EMAIL to config.contact.email so the page really is fed from the single source its comment describes.

trust.title: About page says "a Georgian company" without ever naming it
trust.evidence: Line 61 renders `{t("about.lead")}`, which is "A Georgian company connecting travellers with the people who know these roads best." (src/lib/i18n/en.ts:610). The body paragraphs (lines 75-77) render about.body1-3, which begin "RoutePlanner is a Georgian platform for booking private drivers..." (en.ts:611). `config` is imported at line 6 but used only for `config.appUrl` in generateMetadata (lines 22-23). Nothing on the page names the registered entity, its ID number or its address.
trust.why: The page asserts corporate status — "A Georgian company" — as a trust signal while withholding which company. About/Impressum is the second conventional home for the statutory identity disclosure after the footer, and a reader who follows the footer's "About us" link expecting to learn who they are dealing with learns only the brand. The claim of being a registered Georgian company is verifiable only against an identification number the site never publishes.
trust.fix: Add a short identity line or block at the foot of the About page: `{config.company.legalName} · ID {config.company.idNumber} · {config.company.address}`. Leave about.body1-3 in the brand voice — those are correctly marketing copy.

trust.title: HANDOVER.md still tells the next operator the address is generic and must be replaced
trust.evidence: Line 343: "| `COMPANY_ADDRESS` | Printed in every contract | Still generic — see §12 |"; line 409 (§12 open items, ranked second by importance): "2. **`COMPANY_ADDRESS` is the generic \"თბილისი, საქართველო\"** rather than the registered street address. It prints in every contract. Not blocking, but it should be the real address before volume."
trust.why: src/lib/config.ts:107 now defaults COMPANY_ADDRESS to "Vazha-Pshavela 76, Tbilisi, Georgia", so the open item is closed. Leaving it listed invites someone to "fix" it by hand in the Render dashboard or the new host's environment, which is the one way to get a wrong address back into signed contracts, and it leaves the handover document overstating the outstanding legal work.
trust.fix: Delete open item 2 from §12, renumber the list, and change the §10 note for COMPANY_ADDRESS from "Still generic — see §12" to the configured value or to "defaulted in src/lib/config.ts".

trust.title: The contract render test pins a different entity, so nothing exercises the configured company details
trust.evidence: Lines 16-19: "// config reads the environment once, at module load, so the company details have to exist before anything imports it." / `process.env.COMPANY_LEGAL_NAME ||= 'შპს "რაუტ ჯორჯია"';` / `process.env.COMPANY_ID_NUMBER ||= "437377704";` / `process.env.COMPANY_ADDRESS ||= "თბილისი, საქართველო";`
trust.why: These variables are unset in the test environment, so `||=` assigns — and because a defined env var beats a Zod default, the suite renders every agreement against a third entity: a different identification number (437377704, the same wrong one HANDOVER.md carries) and the generic address the handover says to stop using. HANDOVER.md §11 sells this test as the guard on the contract check people skip, but it now certifies values that are not the ones production prints, and it is the reason the wrong ID number has survived unnoticed in two files.
trust.fix: Delete the three `||=` lines and let the config defaults supply the values, so the test renders the entity production actually contracts as; if a fixture is still wanted for the missing-details path, set it explicitly in that one test rather than at module load.

cosmetic.title: Schema.org provider identity for paid services carries only the brand
cosmetic.evidence:
provider: { "@type": "Organization", name: "RoutePlanner", url: config.appUrl },

emitted inside a "@type": "Service" block that also carries a concrete price and "availability": "https://schema.org/InStock" (lines 96-101). The identical line appears at src/app/[locale]/tours/[slug]/page.tsx:78 inside a "TouristTrip" with an Offer. Both files import config and neither reads config.company.
cosmetic.why: schema.org Organization distinguishes name (the brand, correctly RoutePlanner here) from legalName. Since these blocks advertise a priced, purchasable service, the machine-readable provider record for a commercial offer omits the legal identity that backs it. This is the mildest item on the list: name is not wrong, legalName is simply absent.
cosmetic.fix: Add legalName: config.company.legalName (and optionally taxID: config.company.idNumber and an address node) to the provider object in both files, leaving name as the brand.

cosmetic.title: .env.example still documents the company fields as empty and shows a third, non-existent company name in its MAIL_FROM example
cosmetic.evidence:
# ---- Contracting entity ---------------------------------------------------
# Printed into the driver agreement. The agreement cannot be published for
# signature until all three are set — see src/lib/contract.ts.
COMPANY_LEGAL_NAME=""
COMPANY_ID_NUMBER=""
COMPANY_ADDRESS=""  (lines 42-47), and at line 60: `# MAIL_FROM="Route Planner <noreply@routeplanner.ge>"`
cosmetic.why: Two problems. First, the file still tells an operator the entity is unset and must be filled in, which now contradicts src/lib/config.ts:105-107 where all three have real defaults — anyone copying this to .env sets all three back to "" and re-breaks contract publishing, since missingCompanyDetails() gates on non-empty. Second, the sample MAIL_FROM reads "Route Planner" with a space, which is neither the brand "RoutePlanner" nor the entity "LLC Route Georgia" — a third spelling for the same sender, and the one an operator is most likely to paste into production.
cosmetic.fix: Set the three COMPANY_* lines to the real registered values (or comment them out with a note that config.ts now defaults them and these override only for a rename or move), and correct the MAIL_FROM example to whatever the From line is decided to be.

cosmetic.title: Structured-data Organization declares only the brand name
cosmetic.evidence: `provider: { "@type": "Organization", name: "RoutePlanner", url: config.appUrl },` — and the same literal at src/app/[locale]/tours/[slug]/page.tsx:77. Both are emitted as application/ld+json (transfers line 108-109, tours line 95). Neither reads config.company.
cosmetic.why: Using the brand as schema.org `name` is correct — that is what the Organization is called. But schema.org provides `legalName` and `taxID` precisely so the trading entity behind a brand is machine-readable, and search engines and aggregators use them to match a site to a registered business. Omitting them is a missed disclosure rather than a misstatement, hence lower severity than the footer and legal documents.
cosmetic.fix: Extend both provider objects with `legalName: config.company.legalName` and `taxID: config.company.idNumber` (and optionally an `address` PostalAddress), keeping `name: "RoutePlanner"` as the brand.

cosmetic.title: Contact page hardcodes the support address instead of reading config.contact.email
cosmetic.evidence: `const SUPPORT_EMAIL = "support@routeplanner.ge";` under the comment "Contact details are held in one place so they cannot drift between the footer, the emails and this page. Replace these with real ones before launch" (lines 23-27), then used at line 62. The footer uses `config.contact.email` (src/app/[locale]/layout.tsx:140) and the contracts use `SUPPORT_EMAIL: config.contact.email` (src/lib/contract.ts:132).
cosmetic.why: The comment claims a single source and this file is the one place that is not it — a literal in a page component, invisible to the SUPPORT_EMAIL env var. Change the address in the environment and the footer, the emails and every signed agreement follow while the contact page keeps showing the old one, which is the drift the comment says it prevents. It is also the page where the entity, its identification code and its registered address would naturally be published now that they exist.
cosmetic.fix: Import config and use `config.contact.email` at line 62, deleting the literal; while there, add the entity line (config.company.legalName, idNumber, address) so the registered contracting party is stated somewhere public.
